Pixar will start 2027 off with a major shake-up at the top of its leadership structure, with general manager Jonathan Garson tapped to succeed Jim Morris as president at the studio and veteran producer Jonas Rivera moving into an expanded role as executive vice president of creative.

The appointments will take full effect on January 4, 2027. Pete Docter will continue as chief creative officer, while Morris, who has been studio president since 2014, will become president emeritus as he prepares for eventual retirement.

In his new role, Garson will oversee Pixar’s production and operations, including producers, department heads, and post-production, working alongside Docter. Both Garson and Morris will report to Alan Bergman, chairman of Disney Entertainment, Studios. The new president explained in a release:

I still remember seeing Toy Story for the first time – never imagining I’d one day work at Pixar, let alone step into a leadership role such as this. Every day I walk in the door here, I’m reminded just how special this place is and how lucky I am to be a part of it. Jim has shown me what it looks like to safeguard this culture of quality, innovation, and creative ambition, and I’m extremely grateful to both him and Alan for their trust and support. It’s a humbling opportunity, and I look forward to working with Pete, Jonas, the production leadership team led by Katherine Sarafian and Lindsey Collins, and all of the extraordinary talent here at Pixar as we continue to push boundaries and lead our studio into the future.

Pixar’s incoming president has worked for parent company Disney for more than three decades and joined Pixar in 2010. Before becoming general manager, he helmed the studio’s marketing and franchise team.

“Jim has shown me what it looks like to safeguard this culture of quality, innovation, and creative ambition, and I’m extremely grateful to both him and Alan for their trust and support,” Garson said in the announcement.

Rivera’s appointment comes with a significant shift in responsibilities. When we covered his promotion to executive VP of film production in 2022, his remit was listed as operational oversight of film and streaming production, with Docter handling creative oversight. Now, Rivera will focus full time on the creative side alongside Docter.

Rivera said:

Ever since I walked through these doors as Pixar’s first production intern, this place, its people, and its stories have been my life’s work. I am deeply honored to step into this new role alongside Pete, partnering with him and Jonathan to support our incredible filmmakers and artists. Jim has been an extraordinary mentor and leader, and I intend to build on the lessons I learned from him as we look toward our next chapter.

His responsibilities will now include Pixar’s directors, creative VPs, and development, casting, and content advisement departments. Rivera and Docter will also serve as executive producers on every Pixar film.

Rivera joined Pixar in 1994 as its first production intern. His producing credits include Up, Inside Out, and Toy Story 4, the latter two earning him Oscars. He also executive produced Inside Out 2, the studio’s highest-grossing film ever at the global box office.

As he sheds some of his responsibilities at the studio, Morris will remain executive producer of Incredibles 3. His new role is said to include talent development and mentoring at Pixar and across Walt Disney Studios, along with technology initiatives that support artists and filmmakers.

In a release, the outgoing president reflected on his transformative time at the company:

Leading Pixar has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I’m honored to have been a steward of its legacy alongside extraordinary artists, storytellers, and technologists who keep redefining what animation can do and expanding the art of cinema. After 52 years in the business, and almost 40 at Lucasfilm and Pixar, I’ll be stepping back from the day-to-day, but I’m thrilled to move into handling a number of special projects, working alongside my friends Pete, Jonathan, and Jonas at Pixar, and of course Alan Bergman, who has been such a supporter of Pixar throughout the years.

Looking ahead, I can’t think of anyone better than Jonathan to carry the legacy of this beloved studio forward. He’s a Pixar person through and through, a fierce champion of our films, our people, and our culture. Pixar is in very good hands.

Before joining Pixar in 2005, Morris held senior positions at Industrial Light & Magic and Lucas Digital. His years as Pixar president encompassed both major commercial successes and a difficult period of restructuring as the studio’s parent company reassessed its streaming ambitions and theatrical business.

In May 2024, Pixar cut approximately 175 jobs, or 14% of its workforce, in the largest layoffs in its history. In a staff memo, Morris connected the reductions to Pixar’s retreat from Disney+ series production and renewed focus on features. This year, as Disney embarked on a massive, year-long series of cost-cutting measures, Pixar was hit by a similarly significant round of cuts as it prepared to embrace a “long and lean” production approach, explained to us by a longtime employee as a strategy that will limit future films to 16,500 person-weeks of labor, down from 18,500 to more than 20,000 on previous productions.

January’s upcoming succession plan now places production and operations under Garson while strengthening the creative leadership partnership between Docter and Rivera. Bergman characterized the changes as preparation for Morris’s eventual retirement, although no specific retirement date was announced.

Pixar’s upcoming slate includes the original features Gatto, scheduled for March 5, 2027, and Ghost Market, due March 10, 2028, followed by Incredibles 3 in June 2028.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Busy Bodies, an American production written, directed, and animated by Kate Renshaw-Lewis and produced by Eric Ackerman through Ackzilla Entertainment. The film blends hand-drawn animation with inkjet and screen printing, with each frame printed at approximately 1.5 inches before being enlarged for the screen. It qualified for Oscar consideration by winning the Grand Jury Award for Animated Short at Slamdance.

Inside a domestic factory, tiny workers manufacture disposable objects under the supervision of giant hands. Inspired by Rube Goldberg machines and a “made by hand” sticker on a supermarket wrap, Renshaw-Lewis turns everyday convenience into an elaborate, unsettling production process. The printed sequences progressively deteriorate as they cycle, while a soundtrack built from vintage synthesizers, household objects, and even a pet rabbit’s chewing adds an ominous undertone to the miniature workers’ activities.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Kate Renshaw-Lewis: This was my first film where the choice of medium came first. I had the opportunity to make a film using printed animation, and I wanted to create a narrative that reflected its mechanical, step-by-step process.

The idea for the narrative came to me while I was grabbing lunch during my lunch break, when I noticed a small sticker on my prepackaged tuna wrap that said, “made by hand.” I started wondering: Whose hand? How did they make it? Will I ever know what goes on behind the fluorescently illuminated presentation of the grocery store? I started thinking more and more about the unknown mechanisms and production processes behind everyday, mundane items — things that tend to go unnoticed.

A big inspiration for the film was the salmon cannon tube: a large silicone tube suspended above the water that transports salmon over large dams. It is such a surreal invention that has become part of practical reality. Rube Goldberg machines were another huge inspiration for the film. Their logic felt so important to the film because of its redundancy and delicacy. I think our production systems are absurd when you break them down — very efficient, and very absurd. So much engineering and process goes into delivering something as simple as rubber gloves, or even something as natural as a lemon.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

A small detail that truly saved me hours of work was learning about the contact sheet automation function in Photoshop. I highly recommend looking into it if you’re printing animation or making contact sheets. Big thanks to Sam Gurry and Brian Smee, who shared that knowledge with me.

I also learned that maintaining mystery throughout the narrative feels so incredibly important to me. Busy Bodies follows a strict set of rules, but the film doesn’t explain them. I find it incredibly exciting and fulfilling to watch films that feel like a window into an entire world. I recently watched a retrospective of Jan Švankmajer’s short films that really highlighted this concept for me.

I find it incredibly important to have a very structured mind map and storyboard before beginning production to ground the film, even if the storyboard is only really legible to me. I also really love creating playlists for my films to listen to throughout production.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

I was teaching printed animation classes at the time and had free access to a print studio. Many choices for the film’s visuals and narrative came from the restrictions of the printing process.

The film uses a combination of inkjet printing, using individual color passes, and screen printing. Screen printing requires separate screens burned for each color, which limits the film’s color palette. Because every line, even the still background lines, is printed for every frame, slight variations create a beautiful rhythm, similar to animated boils but with a different tone.

The animation and background style are pretty limited, too, because I knew the final printed frames would be very small and fine detail would be lost. I scaled every frame down to about 1.5 inches so 20 frames could fit on one sheet, then printed them. The paper texture really comes alive because the images are printed so small and then scaled up. The texture in Busy Bodies isn’t noticeable on the printed sheets in person, but it’s a big part of the film’s visual language.

How did you develop the film’s soundtrack, and what role did sound play in shaping its tone?

Most of the sounds in Busy Bodies were recorded at the Vintage Synthesizer Museum in L.A. I went with my two dear friends and incredible musicians, Arius Ziaee and Alex Edgeworth. The three of us spent two straight hours recording a whole library of sounds that I then sampled and built the film’s score from, with help from Arius and Alex.

I also used a keyboard, a clarinet, and a harmonium. I recorded all sounds outside of the synthesizers on my phone in my bedroom during odd hours of the night to avoid street noise. I built the Foley and sound design using recordings of various items, such as vacuums, pillows, water pouring into bowls, sheets of metal, various vintage buttons, and even my pet rabbit chewing hay.

I particularly love the moment when the glove filled with the small workers disappears, and they scatter, running away: All their footsteps are ASMR-style recordings of my fingers tapping on a small piece of wood.

Major sonic inspirations for this film were Raymond Scott, Joe Meek, and Ursula Bogner, who became a key reference point for the film’s sound design. I’m very particular about sound in my films, and I love sound that blends Foley, soundscapes, and music together. It feels incredibly important that the sound adds a subtle, ominous, dark tone to my films. My animation style, and animation in general, can seem quite cute, like a medium intended for children, and I love adding sound that gently nods toward the film’s darker subjects and layers.

Texas’s next attorney general has a far cooler backstory than his job title might suggest.

Democrat Nathan Johnson won Tuesday’s election, along with just about every other Democrat on the ballot across the state, becoming the first Texas AG from his party since 1994. But before entering politics, he composed music for 67 episodes of Funimation’s Dragon Ball Z dub and several of its movies.

If you’re wondering why Dragon Ball Z needed American music in the first place, Funimation believed a more continuous soundtrack would help hold U.S. children’s attention. The company replaced Shunsuke Kikuchi’s original Japanese score with newly commissioned music, eventually bringing in Johnson for its 2005 redub of the opening 67 episodes. In a 2012 interview, Johnson recalled being instructed to provide music throughout, even when he would have preferred. Apparently, saving Earth wasn’t enough. You also had to stop kids from changing the channel.

To celebrate his electoral victory, we spent far too long listening to a YouTube playlist of Johnson’s work today and picked five of our favorites from his work on the franchise.

The selections include music from Fusion Reborn, whose English-language score Johnson created with Dave Moran. Track titles follow the fan uploads below.

5 – “Welcome To Other World”

Dragon Ball Z’s afterlife is equally haunting and charming. Its music box-like chimes and 3/4 time signature help create an ethereal feeling that fits the shocking resutls of yesterday’s elections.


4 – “Goku Powers Up Kaio Ken Attack”

It’s hard not to get hyped up listening to any of Goku’s power-up tracks, and Johnson and his party colleagues must certainly be feeling at their peaks today.


3 – “Vegeta Vs. (Beast) Zarbon”

For those unfamiliar with the scene, negotiations have broken down. Neither party appears interested in mediation. Sounds familiar.

2 – “SSJ3 Goku Vs. Janemba”

Johnson collaborated with musician Dave Moran on Fusion Reborn, combining metal guitar riffs with orchestral scoring.

1 – “Gogeta’s Theme”

Goku and Vegeta put aside their differences, fuse into one person, and get the job done. Wouldn’t it be great if politicians could do the same?

Honorable Mention – “Piccolo’s Sacrifice”

Piccolo is probably my favorite character in all of anime, so he had to make the list somewhere.

Let us know your favorite tracks that came from the pen of Texas’s new AG in the comments below.

Ninety-five years after Dr. Seuss, aka Theodor Geisel, published his first collection of stories in 1931, his works are still read around the globe. His 60 children’s books are masterpieces of wordplay and potent prose that guide generations as they amble toward maturity. One of his most famous books, The Cat in the Hat, debuted in 1957 and captures the joy of childhood chaos and the magic you can make out of boredom.

Following a 2003 live-action adaptation starring Mike Myers, The Cat in the Hat returned to development when Warner Animation Group acquired the rights in 2018. The studio tasked co-writers Erica Rivinoja (Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs 2) and Alessandro Carloni (Kung Fu Panda 3) with co-directing their screenplay, with Bill Hader executive producing and voicing the Cat. In 2024, DNEG Animation came aboard to animate the film, and the result is a fresh interpretation of The Cat in the Hat tailored to modern kids and parents still as bored and disconnected as ever.

First-time director Rivinoja and veteran feature animation director Carloni sat down with Cartoon Brew to discuss the visual choices in their adaptation, their original characters, and how they expanded Geisel’s book into a feature-length tale.

Boosting the Book

From the early days of their screenwriting, Rivinoja says they knew the constraints of Geisel’s The Cat in the Hat needed to be opened up. “The book is very small. It’s one location over one short period of time, and it’s just a few characters,” she says. “But it was important to us that we take that book and those characters that are so beloved and put them on screen.”

She says they asked themselves why the events of the book happened and how the Cat got this weird gig showing up in the homes of bored kids on rainy days. Their answers set up the structure of the screenplay. “This movie’s going to show us that this hat is his company uniform, and he’s actually one of many specialists that entertain children on rainy days,” she explains.

Carloni says that even though they modernized the expanded world of the Cat, they still wanted to feature siblings, older Gabby (Xochitl Gomez) and younger Sebastian (Tiago Martinez), who end up embarking on a journey with the Cat to better appreciate their family.

“In the book, the kids are very much understimulated, just looking at the rain waiting for something to happen. In our movie, we try to overstimulate them,” Carloni says of the kids. “They’re staring at the screen; they’re overwhelmed with games and social media. But the result is the same: disconnection and being uninspired and unmotivated. The Cat represents a force of nature that can come in and allow you to reconnect in the present, in the moment, and with the ones you love. So, in a way, even though we transform the source of the problem from the book, the result is the same: what happens when you disconnect from the here and now and the ones you love, and the Cat comes.”

The HQ, the Apartment, and the Box Worlds

As feature animation continues to explore fresh ways to move beyond established CG house styles, Carloni says they approached their visual decisions by focusing on story.

“This is the only Dr. Seuss book where a whimsical talking Seussian character comes into our world, as opposed to staying in Whoville or the world that Seuss creates,” Carloni points out. “And so, it presented us with the cinematic opportunity to create the real world and the Seussian magical world where he comes from. Then, we go into this magical world through nostalgia and memories. Foolishly, we ended up having three looks of picture, which ended up being such an amazing amount of work. But at least there’s pride in saying that this moment in animation allowed us to explore what the movie should look like, and we grounded that into the narrative necessity of our own story.”

Rivinoja says DNEG’s visual effects supervisor Matt Waters and digital effects supervisor Jean-François Lerouxy were especially important in helping them translate their ideas to the screen, along with production designer Aidan Sugano.

“Sugano had these wonderful ideas about really referencing printing in the Seuss world, so you’ll notice that there’s, like, occasionally print offset marks that you would have had in the books,” Rivinoja says. “There’s occasional paper textures and stuff; it was just so innovative and smart. The care that was given to make it seem like the book came to life was just so beautiful and amazing to me.”

Overall, Carloni says much of their design approach is tied to shape language. “We realized earlier on that we didn’t want to transform the characters themselves. What we wanted to transform is their surfacing, their rendering, their aesthetic, and the color palettes,” he explains. “And above all is the way the light hits. We first started to strip all the occlusion from the Seuss world. But we didn’t want to make the mistake of just going toward toon shading and letting it pretend to be 2D or hand-drawn. A lot of the work came from, we’re going to strip the occlusion and then we’re going to figure out, where is the light source that will give the three-dimensionality?”

He references one of his favorite scenes in the film as an example, where the Cat is being sabotaged by his boss, Mr. Hoogeboom (Giancarlo Esposito), with a potato on a string. “It became simplified, no occlusion, very flat, and then we gave it a bounce from the desk of the boss and it brought up this warm, three-dimensional light onto him. The goal was always to get to a place in which you look at it and you’re like, ‘Wait, what am I looking at? Is this traditional animation? Is it CG, or is it not?’ It was always about finding that balance. First, strip it all down, make it almost look toon-shaded, and then figure out where the softness comes from.”

To distinguish the rest of the HQ area, where all of the various Seussian creatures assemble to get their child assignments, Carloni says they decided to include broken edges everywhere to make sure that the sharp edges of typical surfaces never looked too digital. “There’s this little sense that it’s a brushstroke, or a print offset,” he says of the impression it gives viewers. “It allows the element of organic mannerism to appear on screen, which very much fueled this notion of, ‘What am I looking at right now?’ which I love so much.”

Some Things

Two major additions to this version of The Cat in the Hat are a stalking villain called the Something and a community of Things that extends far beyond the book’s Thing 1 and Thing 2.

“Inherently, when people think of The Cat in the Hat, they think of a young reader book, and so our challenge was always to make it a film for all ages; something that would appeal to adults and not just for little kids,” Rivinoja explains. “With that came the directive, which we were very glad about, to have a real monster, to have real stakes and drama.”

When it came to expanding Geisel’s Things into a whole community of numbered, blue-haired creatures, Carloni admits they were the hardest thing to crack. “Mostly the question for us was, what are they doing on screen?” he explains. “They’re chaotic, but we don’t want just chaos to associate with comedy because that’s not really it. You need to figure out, what are they doing?”

Carloni says it took them a year to figure out the Things’ role, but their eureka moment came when they tried to storyboard a scene with the Things stalking the pet goldfish, Waffles (Matt Berry), for lunch.

“We’re like, ‘It still doesn’t feel amazing,’” he remembers. “We knew that the landlord was a source of problems, and she would bang from below and run upstairs, and that became the idea: what if the [Things] try to communicate? The whole function of the Things for most of the movie is that they’re trying to communicate and it just so happens that their language is hilarious and visual and grounded in rhythmic mayhem. [Sebastian] is trying to communicate back with them, so it becomes a game of charades.

“Once we cracked it, and once we boarded it, and once we put it on screen, it was successful enough that the studio and the executives and everybody else asked us to put more of them in because they were not in the original third act,” he reveals. “But because we finally cracked it, people wanted more of it.”

Rivinoja says it was their head of story, Ryan Gaffney, who first came up with the idea of a rhythmic, nonverbal language for the Things. They then brought in choreographer and body movement expert Christopher Scott (Wicked) to help them develop the Things’ communication.

“He’s so brilliant and was so excited by this idea of a percussive language,” she says. “He got us the most amazing dancers from all walks of life. He got people from Stomp and b-boys and krumpers, and he even had a few ASL dancers who are deaf and who speak sign language to help develop this language.”

Carloni says Dr. Seuss Enterprises enthusiastically approved their big changes to the Things, too. “Technically, we were going to break a standard that stood from 1957 — there’s Thing One and Thing Two, and they look the same. And we said, ‘What if there’s three and seven and 25 and 50, and they all look different from one another?’ And they encouraged us.”

The release of The Cat in the Hat closes a years-long journey for Rivinoja and Carloni, and they’re very proud of the film. “The thing I love the most about our job, and at the same time the thing that is hardest, is not to tell stories but to create characters,” Carloni says. “The fact that the character we’re creating is something that also has lived in people’s homes for generations was exciting and daunting at the same time.

“Working with Erica and with Bill Hader truly shaped someone that I ended up falling in love with,” Carloni says of their Cat. “There’s always a moment working in filmmaking where you feel like you’re creating a character and then at some point, you’re no longer creating, but you meet them. When there are moments like that on screen where one specific line that we wrote was performed in a specific way by a brilliant actor, and then it moved in a specific way by a great animator, suddenly that’s a real person. I feel like that’s where I am with the Cat and I cannot wait for the audience to get to meet him too.”

ROME, Italy — The 12th edition of MIA (Mercato Internazionale Audiovisivo, or International Audiovisual Market) came to a close over the weekend with a strong presence from the international filmmaking community. Over 100 projects from 43 countries were presented across the various programs in Rome, reaffirming MIA as an essential market in the European landscape.

This year, animation was more prominent than ever, with MIA introducing a new gap-financing market for animated series that provided projects from around the world with significant financing and the opportunity to complete their funding with the help of distributors, co-producers, and other financiers. Projects from 24 countries were submitted, with 19 projects representing 15 countries selected for the first edition of the gap-financing market.

Though there was a palpable excitement at the market this year, there was also one recurring feeling — that of uncertainty in changing times. Between mergers, big firings at Netflix, and shrinking budgets, it’s hard to know what the future holds for the industry. Even the question of AI felt like an unspoken specter that virtually everyone refused to acknowledge, while still being very much felt as a concern.

Here are a few takeaways from the 2026 edition of the Rome MIA Market.

International Co-Productions: More Important Than Ever

With the big studios undergoing mergers, there was a palpable sense of concern about the shrinking landscape of places to go to help produce new animated projects. But there was also a clear sense that international co-productions are and will continue to be an important way to make sure new and established voices in the industry get their foot in the door. Going smaller but with more players on board seems to be one workaround to the shrinking of the industry.

Of the projects presented at both the series and feature markets, most titles were international co-productions. Not only was there a sense that going international would help projects get financing faster, but it would also help a project reach new audiences more easily. One notable example was Storie in Viaggio (Stories on the Run), based on a series of books and produced by La Sarraz Pictures. The series was pitched as Love, Death + Robots for kids, an animated journey through Italian myths, traditions, and folklore, with each episode being done by a different animator in a different visual style — from cutout paper to 2D to stop motion. The producers were seeking international partners and talked about the possibilities of going beyond just Italian stories to also explore the local folklore of other countries involved in the production.

New Investment Sources Are Needed

When Cartoon Brew had a chance to speak with MIA director Gaia Tridente after the end of the market, she pressed the issue of financing. “With commissioners becoming more selective and financing structures increasingly complex, producers need to explore new sources of investment and international partnerships,” Tridente told us.

“This is also why we launched the European Investment Hub at MIA 2026, bringing together public institutions, private investors, funds and financial institutions to explore new financing models and improve access to capital across the audiovisual industry. This is particularly relevant to animation, where long production cycles and the development of original IP require substantial investment.”

Audience Definitions Are Blurring

During a children’s pubcaster meeting panel, a report was shared from a closed-door discussion between representatives of various broadcasters in Europe. One of the big topics discussed was that of the increasingly blurred definition of children’s target audiences. The conclusion was that traditional age categories are no longer accurate representations of what children are consuming. It’s always been true that kids will be interested in media aimed at older audiences, but now more than ever, kids are not really responding to the specific targets broadcasters are focusing on. The problem is that if the industry can no longer define its audience accurately, then how can it develop stories that will find the right audience?

This becomes especially tricky when it comes to slightly older audiences, around the 10–14 demographic, where competition for audiences’ attention becomes harder and the offerings slimmer.

A Lack Of Stories For Teens

That same report made it a point to highlight the challenges of reaching the 10–14 audience, mostly due to a lack of European animation for preteens and teenagers. During a panel about the challenges facing animation distribution, Monica Levy from Federation Studios (Ollie & Moon, Kung Fu Wa) talked about the difficulty of producing and selling animation aimed at those ages because broadcasters rely more on live-action titles to cater to teenagers. Not only are audiences growing out of traditional children’s programming and instead discovering projects aimed at older audiences, but public broadcasters in Europe are also struggling to offer enough alternatives to live-action programming or anime. This last bit is important because teens are very much still consuming animation; it’s just not necessarily programming made in Europe.

Seeing the different projects presented at MIA, particularly at the gap-financing market and a presentation about Italian animation, it was clear that the vast majority of projects were aimed at very young audiences, with only a couple meant for older kids or teens. It’s part of why Wildwood feels so special, even if it very much isn’t the first PG-13 animated film. There just aren’t enough.

IP, Brand-Making Remain Crucial

It probably isn’t surprising, but IP remains crucial in ensuring a project gets made. Having some established property to adapt means having data showing that the property has already found success in another medium, and fans who would check out an adaptation. Most of the pitches at the gap-financing market were projects based on books, and considering they already have most of their financing in order, it’s easy to see how having established IP helped. From adaptations of the Juniper Mae and DragoXP books to news of Barry Loser getting an Italian partner right before the show’s presentation at MIA, it’s clear that in these turbulent times, IP is a way to help a project get made.

At the distributors’ panel, Diego Ibáñez Belaustegui from DeAPlaneta Entertainment (Milo) talked about the importance of not only having established IP but also brand-building. For distributors and producers, knowing how to build and expand a brand is important beyond just the initial TV show or film. Belaustegui highlighted the success of Milo in Europe and Bluey in Australia as examples of brands expanding exponentially beyond how they originated to become global phenomena through licensing and international exposure.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Joachim Hérissé’s The Flesh Dress (La Robe peau), a French stop-motion horror story co-written with Emma Degoutte and produced by Stéphanie Launay at Komawé. Featuring original puppets by textile artist Aline Bordereau, the film uses the physical qualities of fabric and flesh to explore aging, control, and artistic creation. It qualified for Oscar consideration by winning Best Animation at LA Shorts 2026.

The story follows an aging tailor whose fear of growing old and attachment to his past take a macabre turn when a disturbing event inspires a new creation. For Hérissé, the premise offered a way to confront bodily anxieties that he finds difficult to express in words, alongside his fear of reproducing patterns of domination. Elaborate camera work and tactile puppet animation give those concerns a physical form, blurring the boundaries between clothing, skin, and the bodies beneath them.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Joachim Hérissé: Stop-motion cinema is the only way for me to express feelings of anguish linked to the body that are very hard for me to verbalize. The fear of aging is a central theme in this film. I believe this fear is one of the driving forces behind many behaviors of domination in human beings — particularly in men, and even more so among creators. As both a man and a creator, I have a deep-seated fear of reproducing these behaviors that have conditioned us since childhood. By making this film, I wanted to examine that fear — perhaps in order to exorcise it?

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

As an author, making this film has had a cathartic effect on me that only dreams — and maybe psychoanalysis? — can trigger. That catharsis began with the writing, alongside my co-writer Emma Degoutte, and developed through directing. I cannot thank my team enough for allowing me to express myself. It now continues to bloom through screenings that spark many deep discussions with audiences.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

Feelings of anguish are very strong in my body. Extremely real. Only the physical material of animation could allow me to echo this hypersensitivity. Only stop-motion cinema could. But I had to find an artistic universe strong enough to resonate with my feelings. Textile artist Aline Bordereau brought me this visual power through her amazing original puppets.

The film blurs the line between fabric, flesh, and skin. What were the biggest technical challenges in making those materials behave convincingly in stop motion?

The first technical challenge is the mise-en-scène. I work extensively on the animatic, using real-time 3D to test and establish quite elaborate framing, camera movements, and editing rhythms that are essential to making the materials behave convincingly.

Then the biggest challenge is finding the perfect stop-motion team: cinematography, production design, puppet making, animation, composition, sound design… I had the chance to work with some of the greatest talents in France.

Luxury fashion’s interest in hand-drawn holiday animation continues, with Dior recruiting The Triplets of Belleville and The Illusionist director Sylvain Chomet for its new Christmas short, “Christian Dior’s Night in Color.”

Set on a snowy winter night in 1949, the film imagines an urgent commission: Marlene Dietrich needs a dress after her Hollywood director decides to shoot in color. Christian Dior and his atelier work through the night to create a gown inspired by the house’s celebrated Junon design. The fictional story draws on the real friendship between the couturier and actress.

Robert Pattinson narrates, with Louis Garrel voicing Dior, Camille Cottin playing Dietrich, and Rihanna appearing as a lucky star. Josh O’Connor voices a chair, while Greta Lee, Nine d’Urso, and Nadia Tereszkiewicz play bees, a nod to the nickname for the house’s seamstresses.

The commission follows Prada’s recent holiday campaign, which enlisted John Pomeroy and fellow traditional animation veterans. Last year’s Don Bluth-inspired Scandinavian recycling PSA offered another memorable example of advertisers finding value in expressive, lovingly crafted 2D animation. And in 2022, Givenchy enlisted Disney legend Eric Goldberg to oversee a 101 Dalmatians–themed ad campaign.

Like those other examples, the Dior ad also came with a behind-the-scenes video. Seen below:

 

View this post on Instagram

 

A post shared by Dior Official (@dior)

For Dior, the connection makes a ton of sense. Both couture and hand-drawn animation depend on skilled artists turning drawings into something audiences can feel. And few filmmakers have as illustrious a resume as Choment when it comes to doing so with real characters from history.

Two siblings cross a nuclear exclusion zone carrying their grandmother’s ashes. It’s a premise rooted in loss, but director François-Marc Baillet sees Back to Tomioka as an adventure: funny, tender, and concerned with how a fractured family finds its way back together amid the ruins of Fukushima.

For Baillet, the connection was personal: he lives near a nuclear power plant, has two children around the same age as his protagonists, and was unable to attend his own grandmother’s funeral during the COVID lockdown.

A research trip to Fukushima helped shape the film’s visual approach, which pairs bold graphic novel stylings with the dust, dense vegetation, and abandoned spaces of a region still living with the disaster’s aftermath.

Here’s a look at the film’s project trailer from Cartoon Movie 2023:

Produced by Foliascope and co-produced by Crunchyroll, the 2D feature is slated for 2028. Its long development also yielded a graphic novel by Michaël Crouzat, Laurent Galandon, and Aude Soleilhac, which the film now adapts. With the project selected for this year’s TIFFCOM, Cartoon Brew spoke with Baillet about finding the film’s own visual language, telling a Japanese story as a European filmmaker, and why making the movie means having to “kill” the comic book.

Cartoon Brew: Tell us how this project began.

François-Marc Baillet: This project began with a movie script written by Laurent Galandon. As financing animation is a long process, the decision was made to create the graphic novel with Michaël Crouzat originally attached to direct the movie. Michaël delivered the comic but left the project after making this amazing teaser in 2022. I was co-directing 2D animation on The Inventor at Foliascope, and [producer] Ilan offered me [the opportunity] to direct and become the graphic author for the feature. I’m not Japanese. I’ve never experienced an earthquake, tsunami, or nuclear accident, but I read the script, and I immediately saw a part of myself in it. I have two kids the age of the two main characters. I live 20 kilometers from a nuclear power plant, and on top of that, in 2020, during the COVID lockdown, I was not allowed to attend my grandmother’s funeral. Why didn’t I disobey like the two kids are doing? I was hooked, and yes, I had to do it!

How did your experience in the region shape the project?

As it is a relatively recent event, the triple catastrophe of Fukushima has been documented a lot. You can find documentaries, tons of pictures, testimonies, and videos from people who lived there or people who traveled into the restriction zone. It’s precious, and it’s helping a lot, but going to Fukushima was indispensable. First, we met Naoto Matsumura, the farmer who helps the kids in our story. He disobeyed for real in 2011 and stayed in the radioactive exclusion zone to take care of the abandoned animals. He is the original spark that made Laurent write the script. He shared with us the extreme loneliness he’d experienced, and he showed us his farm, his life. The week we spent in Tomioka, Namie, Futaba, and Minamisoma exposed me to this dissonance I want to put on screen in my film. Only 20% of people came back 12 years later. We visited a middle school— there used to be 600 students, and now there are just one or two classes left. You can still feel the tragedy. We also experienced radioactivity, and we kept checking the dosimeter to see if there was danger or not, exactly what the characters are experiencing in the film.

The aesthetic is shared with the graphic novel, but it’s striking how, in motion, the film has a photoreal feel.

There was no rotoscoping used in the teaser, nor will there be in the movie, but I’ll keep this semirealistic kind of look that was established for the teaser. Back to Tomioka is not a documentary about a nuclear incident; it is an adventure— funny and tender. Along the way, two orphans, brother and sister torn apart by grief, slowly learn to become family again. Their fragile bond is growing back through the ruins.

I want to frame and illuminate this emotional journey using my painting and color skills to bring the audience with us. 2D animation allows you to choose what you draw and what you don’t; rotoscoping would put you in a different process. I want texture, dust, dense vegetation, and to make this world I’m [portraying] as respectful as possible to what happened there.

It’s striking that this is a project that takes existing illustrations with a cinematic sensibility and brings them to the screen.

One of the challenges in accepting the project was having this comic book already there. This may seem a bit violent, but you have to “kill” the comic book to make the movie happen. The comic can be read in 20 minutes— the rhythm for the audience is radically different when you sit in a movie theater. It’s a different medium, and I had to really work on that idea to create the animatic that we have now almost finished. Putting music, moving the camera, recording voices— very quickly you enter a very different experience.

Tell me about your team.

Caroline Cherrier was a great help in leading the storyboard team at the end of 2025. I continued storyboarding until recently to get the final version of the animatic. Then, yes, it’s constant collaboration, bouncing ideas around with all the artists who will be involved in this production. I studied illustration in school—I’ll take care to keep that touch for the film, but in a different way than the comic. A big part of that is happening during compositing.

What’s it been like pitching an international project with Japanese cultural roots here in Tokyo?

I wasn’t involved in the pitching myself, but I can say that we are really proud to take part in TIFFCOM in Tokyo. Ghibli and Japan took inspiration from European culture (Porco Rosso, Kiki, etc.) to create masterpieces of animation, and we were raised with this rich mix between our cultures. We are proud to enter this path and mix our cultures to tell a story that we hope will inspire the younger generation.

What are your hopes for how this film will impact and speak to international and Japanese audiences?

There is this line of dialogue at the end of the film that sums it up: “We don’t choose what happens to us, but we can choose what we want to protect.” I hope that line travels beyond Japan. Everyone has something to protect: a family, a place, a memory. And I hope parents and children can watch the film together and talk about it afterward.

For Japanese audiences, my hope is humbler. I’m not Japanese, and I know I’m telling a story about a tragedy that others lived. Empathy—trying to understand what others are experiencing—seems key in this crazy life. What I try to do is listen, read, go there, meet Naoto Matsumura and the people of the region, and stay as faithful as I can to what I saw and felt. If people from Tomioka or Fukushima watch the film and feel that their land and their story were treated with respect, that would mean more to me than anything else.

Welcome to Cartoon Brew’s series of spotlights focusing on the animated shorts that have qualified for the 2027 Oscars. The films in this series have qualified through one of multiple routes: by winning an Oscar-qualifying award at a film festival, by exhibiting theatrically, or by winning a Student Academy Award.

Today’s short is Amos Sussigan’s Pigeons, a Swiss-American production from The Hub Media and BMC Films, narrated by Andy Serkis. Around 45 artists worked across countries and time zones to complete the film in just one year, combining painted backgrounds, CG characters, and traditional 2D effects. The short qualified for Oscar consideration through theatrical exhibition.

A carrier pigeon loses his livelihood when a telephone arrives in his owner’s home, sending him out in search of food, shelter, and a new purpose. Presented in the framework of a traditional nature documentary, the short explores what progress means for those it leaves behind. For Sussigan and his collaborators, the bird’s predicament offered a way to address their own anxieties about automation, creative displacement, and an industry changing around them.

Cartoon Brew: What was it about this story or concept that connected with you and compelled you to direct the film?

Amos Sussigan: It all started with an article I read about carrier pigeons during the war, and a comment from a friend who said, “Just like us with AI.” There was something incredibly sad to me about an animal that had once played such an important role in history suddenly becoming obsolete.

With everything happening in the animation industry around AI and automation, the idea felt incredibly relevant, and I couldn’t stop thinking about it. I loved the idea of telling a story about purpose, identity, and what happens when the world moves on without you. The short is called Pigeons, but ultimately it’s about us.

What did you learn through the experience of making this film, either production-wise, filmmaking-wise, creatively, or about the subject matter?

We were around 45 artists scattered across the world, many of us working nights and weekends, and somehow we managed to complete a 12-minute animated film in around 12 months with almost no budget.

I learned that limitations can actually be incredibly liberating creatively, and that organization, trust, and a little stubbornness can go a very long way.

Most importantly, especially given where we find ourselves with AI, I was reminded that even if people argue that a creative mind can be replaced, determination is much harder to replace. A group of artists who genuinely care about something can still come together and create something deeply human. That is exactly what we did.

Can you describe how you developed your visual approach to the film? Why did you settle on this style and technique?

We turned our limitations into part of the visual language of the film while also trying to pay homage to the history of animation itself.

We had no real budget and no render farm, so we needed to find something visually distinctive but achievable. I’ve always loved the imperfect quality of films like 101 Dalmatians, particularly the Xerox linework and the slightly offset painted backgrounds.

We combined 2D backgrounds, 3D characters, and traditional 2D effects. We also used wide lenses and often framed the world from the pigeons’ point of view, making them feel even smaller and more abandoned within it.

The palette was deliberately filled with pigeon grays, while many background characters remained completely still, painted directly into the environments. Those choices came partly from necessity, but they ultimately became an important part of the film’s identity.

Why did the documentary format fit the story you wanted to tell? And was it always your intent to have a narrator?

I always imagined the short almost like an Animal Planet documentary, observing pigeons as a species trying to adapt to a changing world.

What appealed to me about that approach is that nature documentaries don’t necessarily judge what is happening. Things evolve, species adapt, and sometimes they don’t. In our film, the telephone isn’t the villain—it’s simply progress.

The narrator was part of the concept from the beginning. From a practical perspective, I also knew narration could help us communicate certain moments clearly if we didn’t have the resources to animate everything as extensively as we might have liked.

Having worked with Andy Serkis before, I knew he could bring exactly the balance we needed. He can sound incredibly dark and authoritative, but he can also feel like a grandfather explaining pigeons to his grandson. He brings gravitas and humor without overdramatizing what is happening, which was exactly the tone we wanted.

This month, Cartoon Brew is inviting you to a special For Your Consideration screening of Netflix’s animated feature In Waves in Hollywood on Saturday, November 7, followed by a Q&A and a small reception.

Adapted from AJ Dungo’s autobiographical graphic novel, In Waves follows AJ, a shy teenager who loves drawing and skateboarding but is terrified of the ocean, and Kristen, a surfer who introduces him to the sport and helps him overcome his phobia. As the two navigate life as a young couple and their relationship deepens, a sudden illness turns their hopes and dreams upside down. The couple finds strength in their friends, their love for each other, and their shared passion for surfing, as they face an uncertain and sometimes cruel future.

Directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen, the film features the voices of Will Sharpe and Stephanie Hsu and opened this year’s Cannes Critics’ Week, where it was Netflix’s first deal of the French festival.

TOKYO, Japan – With Laika’s latest production, Wildwood, in its third week of release—having added 150 screens during its second week for a total of 3,103 across the U.S. and Canada. We caught up with Jason Brenek, CEO of the film’s distributor, Fathom Entertainment, in Japan at the Tokyo International Film Festival.

Asked what made Wildwood the distributor’s choice for its first traditional wide release, Brenek, appointed to his role back in July, says, “Human-driven creativity is something that we’ve always been big in, whether it’s been in anime or in stop-motion animation. And we’ve had a long-standing relationship with Laika over the years, where we have rereleased the films that they’ve done, Coraline being an example, on an annual basis to serve that audience and bring that film back to the big screen so that people can see it annually.”

Those re-releases and anniversary screenings established a strong relationship between the companies. Of their latest collab, Brenek notes that Wildwood had been in development for 16 years.

“They had built a real understanding through these anniversary releases that we had done and these bringbacks,” he says. “They knew that they had the base of an audience that they were serving. They also felt, after working within the studio system, the traditional Hollywood system, for the entirety of their existence, that they wanted to have a creative hand in how to reach that audience, how to actually bring their content to their biggest fans. And that was something that they didn’t feel that they could get through the traditional studio system—where oftentimes films, television programs are put together by production companies, thrown over the wall to their distribution entity, the studio, and then the studio says, ‘We’ve got it from here. Don’t worry about it. We’re going to go and market. We’re going to create the art. We’re going to create the trailers.’”

Brenek says Fathom’s approach gives Laika more control over marketing and communication with its fan base, while also allowing it to take advantage of Fathom’s ownership structure.

“Fathom is owned by the three largest cinema chains in the U.S.: Regal, Cinemark, and AMC, representing half the screens in the country. And so we went to our ownership and said, ‘We have this opportunity to do something really big with this partner who we know very well, and let’s try to see how big we can go.’ And so the 3,000 theaters, the wide release, the biggest release that we’ve ever done to date in the 20-year history. We really didn’t know how the film was going to look. We had seen pieces of it along the way, but the passion and the artistry that Laika put behind the film really shows on the screen.”

Reflecting on the film’s second week of release, Brenek points to a “massive desire for human-driven creativity and artistry” amid the entertainment industry’s increasing use of AI. Wildwood grossed an estimated $9 million in its second domestic weekend, an impressive 27% drop from its debut, bringing its 10-day total to $27.4 million. Audience polling supplied by Fathom was similarly encouraging: 96% of moviegoers rated the film excellent or very good, and 87% said they would definitely recommend it.

“The timing of this film coming out in the midst of all of that, where 16 years of love and care and attention to detail of these puppets and stop-motion animation really is hitting at the right time,” he says.

Brenek says “consumers can see something that has heart.” He adds that Fathom has observed that “Gen Z and millennials are seeing theaters as a third space to meet with like-minded fans and come together in a way that they hadn’t for the past 10 years.”

He says interest in “human-driven” art also extends to film formats, including 35mm and 70mm releases, pointing to The Odyssey. Discussing moviegoing more broadly, he also cites A24’s You Can See Everything.

“It’s amazing to release a film at a time where it looks like everything is predictable in terms of what your release schedule is,” he says, “and then something can come out of left field like this documentary that sucks up a lot of oxygen in the room.”

Brenek believes Wildwood has a long life ahead of it, with its critical reception and awards potential potentially extending its theatrical run. He also suggests that audiences’ appreciation for handmade films endures, citing Studio Ghibli’s hand-drawn work.

When deciding what kind of release a film will receive, Brenek says, “There is a need for scale. We’re different than a Neon or an A24. We’re not an independent film studio in that we’re booking theaters for releases of 100 screens or 300 screens. We have a natural threshold around 1,000. If something can play to 1,000 screens, we know that it’s going to satisfy our three owners.”

The second factor is the competitive marketplace: what a film would face on its opening weekend.

“This year has been bonkers from a content flow standpoint,” he says. “I think everybody’s realizing that there’s a hunger for new stories, new projects. And so with the success of Obsession, with the success of Backrooms, all of which started in a user-generated space with content creators, people are thinking about theatrical releases with a lower production price point.”

He continues, “I do think the second factor is what’s happening within the marketplace, because we don’t want to take away from other big projects that are coming out. So we’ll figure out the timing of the release.”

The final consideration is marketing.

“What is it going to take for us to market it effectively?” he says. “In the case of Wildwood, Laika had a very clear vision of how to market and promote this film, and you’ll notice that in a lot of the trailers and promotional materials, not a ton was given away.”

Beyond Wildwood, Fathom is finding theatrical audiences for animation that originated online, including The Amazing Digital Circus, whose box office performance caught even Brenek by surprise.

“I think [that was] a surprise to everyone in the industry. I can’t say there was anyone other than probably two people on our team, and the creators of Amazing Digital Circus, and the fans of Amazing Digital Circus who knew how that was going to play in theaters,” Brenek says. “No one thought that it would do the type of business that it did. I mean, it ended up making $25 million at the box office, and it kept going and going and going. And we just didn’t see it. We didn’t get it, which is part of why, as I’ve come in and looked at the industry and the trends that are happening, I think we have to have younger people out in the market finding content that resonates for younger viewers.”

Brenek credits two members of his team who championed the release. Following The Amazing Digital Circus and the success of Obsession, Iron Lung, and Backrooms, he says, “There’s a lot of activity in the industry trying to find similar creators who can tell stories on a big canvas in the theaters,” with Instagram and YouTube serving as a feeder system.

“We do have intentions and have conversations actively with many content creators who are out there to try to find what is the next thing that can justify someone leaving the home, plopping down $20 and seeing something in a theater with a lot of other fans,” he says.

Fathom is also considering more ways to build special events around screenings.

“I think we need to be cognizant when we’re releasing content in theaters that it delivers a certain amount of value. One of the things that we do to add to that value is special Q&A sessions with the creators, or extra footage that you haven’t seen before, or behind-the-scenes, or teasing a new release. I think we’re going to be doing more of that. So just putting the film out, I think not anyone can do that, but that’s something that a lot of people can do directly.”

Brenek says Fathom’s “eventization of content” can also be built around entire franchises.

“For example, we brought back the Lord of the Rings trilogy a couple of times over the last couple of years, the extended versions,” he says. “We know that Lord of the Rings fans are not only into the films, but they’re into cosplay, they’re into merchandise, collectibles. They’re into being a part of, or more immersed in, the world. And so one of the things that we’ve done quite a bit is lean into those collectibles and other types of merchandise to make it a little bit different, and encourage dress-ups, or for certain types of content, have the theaters make certain special drinks that go along with the film, so that it can be all part of the experience that, especially younger people, I think, are looking for.”

When people leave the house, Brenek says, they want “IRL experiences that are unique, that are Instagrammable.” Fathom is looking for ways to “make this thing an event and turn theaters into a third space that no longer really exists for younger people.”

Looking ahead to Fathom’s growth in the coming months and years, Brenek says, “We are looking at what we do well. What audiences do we serve? What audiences do we think have growth potential and are feeling underserved from the amount of content?”

“This is one of the reasons why I’m here in Tokyo with our team,” he adds. “For the 20 years that we have existed, we have been the largest distributor of Japanese animation and anime products into United States theaters. And so taking that subculture, people who are avid fans in the United States for animation and anime out of Japan, we are doubling down on that demographic and trying to bring more in a timelier manner, so that they’re not waiting a year for something.”

Brenek points to a digitally connected global anime audience as a reason for more timely releases.

“Frankly, one of the things that I think a lot of Japanese production companies and creatives aren’t aware of—because it goes through multiple layers of bureaucracy and production committees and all these things just to get projects made and released in Japan—I don’t think they realize necessarily that at the end of that chain in America, it is almost always Fathom releasing that product into theaters. So I guess this is to say that we want to connect more with these demographic groups, and as a result, we’re connecting much more closely with these production entities and creatives in places in the world that are responsible for such amazing artistic works. Another is the creative online community that we talked about. That’s another area that we’re getting heavily into.”

The Association of Japanese Animations (AJA) has announced the name, date, and venue for its previously announced international anime awards program, with the inaugural Nippon Anime Awards set for November 21, 2027, at Tokyo’s SGC Hall Ariake.

The organization revealed the details on Monday, November 2, during the closing event of Tokyo Anime Next, a four-day program held alongside the Tokyo International Film Festival and its TIFFCOM market.

The Nippon Anime Awards are being established to recognize outstanding anime productions and the artists behind them. The goal, according to its inaugural backers, is to reach audiences both in Japan and internationally. Alongside the ceremony, AJA plans to collaborate with the Tokyo Metropolitan Government on initiatives supporting new business opportunities and the development of emerging talent.

In a release, the organization explained:

The name “Nippon Anime Awards” reflects our commitment to honoring the history and culture of Japanese anime while carrying its enduring appeal into the future. The awards will recognize outstanding anime works and celebrate the achievements of those involved in the industry, sharing the appeal of Japanese anime with audiences in Japan and around the world. The aim is to establish the Nippon Anime Awards as a leading anime awards program representing Japan that will be loved and celebrated for years to come.

“We hope to share the appeal and potential of anime to an even wider audience around the world and build that future together with all of you,” AJA president Kazuko Ishikawa elaborated during the announcement.

Tokyo Governor Yuriko Koike also pledged local support in a message shared at the event: “The Tokyo Metropolitan Government will continue to provide strong support for anime and everyone involved in bringing it to life.”

Award categories, eligibility requirements, and details on the voting and selection process were not revealed in this week’s announcement, but with a year to go before the inaugural edition, we’ll keep you posted as we learn more.

Disney is once again planning to eliminate thousands of jobs, continuing a year of repeated redundancies and broader employee-unfriendly cuts under new CEO Josh D’Amaro, even as the company commits billions to shareholder payouts and allocates substantial sums to new AI hires and tech upgrades.

According to Bloomberg, higher-ups have asked some managers to find ways to cut annual costs by 20%. Those savings, the report says, could come from job cuts and other expense reductions, with some parts of the company expected to be hit harder than others. To be clear, the 20% refers to cost savings, not a companywide target to eliminate 20% of Disney’s workforce.

D’Amaro reportedly intends to reinvest a portion of the savings in film and TV programming, technology, theme parks, and cruise ships. Disney declined to comment to Bloomberg. Neither the report nor Disney has specified the exact number of jobs to be eliminated or which operations will bear the brunt of the layoffs.

For Disney employees and the industry at large, this is becoming a painfully familiar routine in 2026. The company eliminated approximately 1,000 positions in April and hundreds more in July, followed by additional cuts in September. Those layoffs followed job losses tied to the consolidation of its marketing operations announced in January.

At Pixar alone, roughly 150 employees lost their jobs in July, despite a strong box-office year led by Hoppers and Toy Story 5.

Remaining employees have seen their benefits take a hit, too. Starting in 2027, Disney will restrict spousal health coverage when spouses can obtain insurance through their own employers, even if the alternative offers worse benefits.

This year’s constant cuts have hardly coincided with an economic downturn at Disney. In its fiscal third quarter, Disney reported $25.25 billion in revenue, up 7%, and $5.6 billion in operating income across its business segments, up 21%. It also raised its annual share-buyback target to at least $9 billion.

And last month, reports revealed that Disney planned to spend roughly $180 million over three years to compensate and retain 66 recruits from bankrupt chatbot company Character.AI, following its former CEO, Karandeep Anand, to Disney. That followed a proposed $1 billion investment in OpenAI, announced alongside a Sora licensing agreement in December 2025, that collapsed just over three months later, before any money changed hands.

We’ve seen nothing to establish that AI spending is directly driving these layoffs, but the company’s priorities are clear from where it is increasing spending and where it has chosen to cut costs.

There is money to reward shareholders, recruit AI talent, and invest in technology. For the employees already making its films, working in its parks, running its operations, and supporting its businesses, the directive is overwhelmingly clear: do more with less. At least for those still around.
